title: Two Ways to Count Crime
objective: After this level you can explain why police records and victim surveys give different crime numbers and what each misses.
summary: Police records count only crimes reported to them. The victim survey asks people directly, finds fewer than half of violent crimes reported, but can't count murders.

cards.headline: Ask how much crime there is, and the US government gives two answers.
cards.body: One count comes from police records, the other from asking people directly. They don't match, and they aren't meant to. Each catches crimes the other misses.

cards.headline: Count 1: crimes reported to police
cards.body: The FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting program, begun in 1929, gathers crimes reported to law enforcement agencies, with counts down to cities and towns. It's local and detailed. But it can only count what reaches the police. A stolen bike nobody reports never makes it into the numbers.

cards.headline: Count 2: ask the people
cards.body: The National Crime Victimization Survey, run since 1973, asks about 240,000 people age 12 or older, in about 150,000 households, whether they were victims of crime, reported or not. In 2024 it found about 23 violent victimizations per 1,000 people, but only about 11 per 1,000 were reported to police. Fewer than half ever reached the first count.

cards.context: It relies on interviews with victims, so homicide is out, and so are crimes against businesses. Police records catch those, but miss everything unreported. Neither is the true number on its own. Together they give a fuller picture.

cards.headline: Crime counts: compared
learned: Police records: crimes reported to law enforcement
Victim survey: asks people, reported or not
Fewer than half of violent crimes are reported

questions.prompt: Why can't the National Crime Victimization Survey count murders?

options.label: Murders are too rare to measure
options.rationale: Rarity isn't the reason; the method is.

options.label: The FBI keeps those numbers secret
options.rationale: The FBI publishes homicide counts; the survey simply can't collect them.

options.label: It only covers crimes against businesses
options.rationale: It's the reverse: businesses are left out.

options.label: It relies on interviews with victims

questions.explanation: The survey asks victims what happened to them, so it cannot include homicide.

questions.prompt: Match each with its fact about counting crime.
questions.explanation: The FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting program began in 1929. The National Crime Victimization Survey, run since 1973, asks about 240,000 people age 12 or older in about 150,000 households.

questions.prompt: The victim survey reports crime per 1,000 people rather than as totals. Why?

options.label: Because the survey's total counts are kept secret
options.rationale: Totals are published too; they just can't compare fairly.

options.label: Because exactly 1,000 people are interviewed in the survey each year
So years and places with different populations compare fairly
To make crime look smaller than police records suggest
options.rationale: A rate describes crime per person; it doesn't hide it.

questions.explanation: Totals grow with population. A rate per 1,000 people puts different years and places on the same footing.
